tagline: Turn raw information into clear evidence people can use.
overview: Analytics and data careers focus on answering practical questions with information. Professionals clean datasets, investigate patterns, build reports or predictive models, and explain what the results mean for a business, hospital, government agency, research team, or nonprofit. The work combines statistics, technology, and communication, but not every position requires advanced machine learning. Many entry-level analysts begin with spreadsheets, SQL, dashboards, and basic statistical methods before moving into more technical modeling.
career_themes: Turning raw data into useful information
typical_tasks: Collect data from spreadsheets, databases, surveys, or business systems
Clean missing, duplicated, or inconsistent records
Write SQL queries and analyze data with Excel, Python, or R
Build dashboards, charts, reports, and statistical models
Check whether results and models are accurate
Present findings and recommendations to decision-makers

education.graduate_school_note: A bachelor's degree is sufficient for many analyst, data visualization, market research, and operations research positions. A master's degree is more valuable for statistician, biostatistics, advanced modeling, and research-focused roles.
education.licensing_or_certification: No license is generally required. Technical certifications may support a resume, but projects, internships, and demonstrated software skills usually provide stronger evidence of readiness.

salary.variability_note: This is a broad national annual-pay range covering many analyst through experienced technical roles. Industry, location, specialization, and experience create major differences. Entry-level positions may fall below the range, while experienced data scientists and specialized modelers can earn substantially more.

advantages: Analytics skills transfer across finance, healthcare, marketing, government, technology, and research.
Many analyst positions are accessible with a bachelor's degree and a strong project portfolio.
Projects can demonstrate concrete ability before a student has extensive professional experience.
The work often produces measurable recommendations that affect real decisions.
Computer-based responsibilities make remote and hybrid arrangements possible in many organizations.
tradeoffs: Cleaning and validating data may take more time than building models or dashboards.
Incomplete or poorly collected data can limit the quality of an analysis.
Job titles are inconsistent, so two data analyst positions may require very different skills.
Deadlines and last-minute requests can create pressure or overtime.
Technical findings must be explained to people who may not understand statistics.
Advanced statistical and research positions may require graduate education.
student_next_steps: Complete a project that cleans, analyzes, and visualizes a real dataset
Learn SQL and one analysis language such as Python or R
Publish the project with a short explanation of the question, method, and result
Practice presenting one chart and one recommendation to a nontechnical audience
Apply for analyst internships across several industries, not only technology companies

tagline: Understand an audience and turn attention into measurable demand.
overview: Marketing and advertising careers connect products, services, and ideas with the people most likely to value them. Professionals research customers, create campaigns, write and review content, manage digital channels, and measure whether their work produces awareness, engagement, leads, or sales. The field combines creativity with business strategy and data, so strong marketers must understand both what attracts people and what produces measurable results.
typical_tasks: Research customer needs, behaviors, and preferences
Plan advertising, email, content, or social media campaigns
Write or review advertisements and promotional content
Coordinate work with designers, sales teams, and clients
Track campaign spending, conversions, and engagement
Present campaign results and recommend improvements

education.graduate_school_note: A bachelor's degree is sufficient for most entry-level marketing, advertising, content, and research positions. Graduate study is more useful for advanced analytics, strategy, and leadership roles.
education.licensing_or_certification: No license is generally required. Platform certifications in advertising, analytics, CRM, or email marketing can support a portfolio but do not replace practical campaign experience.

salary.variability_note: Entry-level assistants and coordinators may earn below this range. Experienced marketing managers, advertising managers, and specialized analytics leaders can earn substantially more.

advantages: Marketing exists across nearly every industry, from sports and technology to healthcare and nonprofits.
Students can demonstrate ability through campaigns, content, research, and portfolio projects.
The field combines creative work with data and business strategy.
Skills can transfer into sales, communications, product management, and entrepreneurship.
Digital marketing responsibilities often support remote or hybrid work.
tradeoffs: Campaign deadlines and public launches can create pressure.
Performance is often judged through visible metrics such as leads, sales, or engagement.
Platform algorithms and advertising tools change frequently.
Some entry-level roles involve repetitive scheduling, reporting, or content production.
Client preferences may override a marketer's preferred creative direction.
student_next_steps: Create a sample campaign for a campus organization or local business
Build a portfolio containing written content, research, and campaign results
Learn one advertising platform and one analytics platform
Track measurable outcomes such as clicks, sign-ups, or sales
Apply for marketing, communications, or customer-research internships

tagline: Use clinical knowledge and evidence to improve people's health.
overview: Healthcare includes direct patient care, diagnostics, rehabilitation, clinical research, health education, and medical data work. Depending on the role, professionals may examine patients, support procedures, analyze test results, document care, study health outcomes, or help patients understand treatment. Education requirements vary sharply because the category includes entry-level support positions, licensed therapists, researchers, nurses, and advanced medical professionals.
career_themes: Assessing patient needs and health conditions
Providing treatment, therapy, or clinical support
Improving care through research and evidence
typical_tasks: Collect patient histories, measurements, or test results
Support examinations, treatments, or rehabilitation
Document care in medical records or health systems
Coordinate with clinicians, researchers, and families
Explain procedures, findings, or next steps to patients
Follow safety, privacy, and infection-control procedures

education.graduate_school_note: Support, community-health, research-coordination, and health-data roles may be accessible without graduate school. Speech-language pathology, advanced nursing, medicine, psychology, and many diagnostic or therapeutic careers require graduate or professional education.
education.licensing_or_certification: Licensing or certification is required for many clinical roles. Requirements depend on the occupation and state, while research, administrative, and health-data positions may not require a clinical license.

salary.variability_note: Healthcare has unusually wide salary variation. Support positions may fall near or below the minimum, while advanced practice nurses, physicians, surgeons, and specialized clinical leaders can earn well above the maximum.

advantages: The work can produce a direct and visible effect on patients and families.
Healthcare offers clinical, research, technology, administrative, and community-service paths.
Many occupations have clearly defined education and advancement routes.
Health knowledge remains useful across hospitals, schools, laboratories, government, and nonprofits.
Specialization allows professionals to focus on particular populations or health conditions.
tradeoffs: Many clinical careers require licensing, graduate education, or supervised training.
Shift work, emergencies, and staffing shortages can create difficult schedules.
Professionals may regularly encounter illness, trauma, grief, or frustrated patients.
Documentation and regulatory requirements take time away from direct care.
Most patient-facing positions cannot be performed remotely.
recommended_course_ids: Neurology for Communication Sciences and Disorders
student_next_steps: Shadow or interview a professional in one healthcare occupation
Earn CPR or Basic Life Support certification when appropriate
Volunteer in a hospital, clinic, rehabilitation center, or community program
Compare the education and licensing requirements of three possible roles
Apply for clinical, research, public-health, or health-data experience

tagline: Turn business data into dashboards, reports, and better decisions.
overview: Business intelligence professionals organize company data so employees and leaders can understand performance and make decisions. They build dashboards, define performance measures, maintain reporting systems, investigate unexpected results, and explain what the numbers mean for areas such as sales, finance, healthcare, operations, or customer service. Compared with broader data science, BI usually places more emphasis on reliable reporting, business systems, and decision support than experimental modeling.
career_themes: Connecting data from different business systems
typical_tasks: Meet with teams to define reporting needs and performance measures
Query databases and combine information from multiple systems
Build dashboards, recurring reports, and data models
Check reports for missing, duplicated, or inconsistent information
Investigate changes in sales, costs, customers, or operations
Present findings to managers and other stakeholders

education.graduate_school_note: A bachelor's degree in information systems, analytics, business, computer science, or a related field is sufficient for many BI analyst roles. Graduate study is more useful for advanced architecture, strategy, or leadership positions.
education.licensing_or_certification: No license is generally required. Power BI, Tableau, cloud, database, and analytics certifications can support a resume, but employers still expect practical SQL, reporting, and dashboard experience.

salary.variability_note: Entry-level reporting roles may fall below this range. Senior BI developers, database architects, consultants, and BI leaders may earn substantially more.

advantages: BI combines technical work with visible business applications.
The skills apply across finance, healthcare, retail, government, and other industries.
Dashboards and reporting projects provide concrete portfolio evidence.
A bachelor's degree is sufficient for many analyst positions.
Computer-based responsibilities often support remote or hybrid work.
tradeoffs: A large portion of the work involves cleaning data and correcting reporting problems.
Different departments may disagree about how a performance measure should be defined.
Legacy databases and poorly connected systems can limit what analysts can produce.
Recurring reports may become repetitive after they are established.
Professionals are expected to understand both technical systems and business needs.
student_next_steps: Build a dashboard using a real business or campus dataset
Learn SQL and one visualization platform
Define useful performance measures before creating visualizations
Practice explaining a dashboard to someone without a technical background
Apply for BI, reporting, business-analyst, or operations-analyst internships

tagline: Organize people, projects, and operations to turn plans into results.
overview: Business and management careers focus on coordinating the people, money, schedules, and processes needed to accomplish an organization's goals. Professionals may manage projects, improve operations, support employees, advise clients, allocate resources, or lead departments. Entry-level graduates usually begin in analyst, coordinator, specialist, or rotational positions before taking responsibility for an entire team or business unit.
career_themes: Leading people through decisions and change
typical_tasks: Set project goals, schedules, responsibilities, and deadlines
Monitor budgets, staffing, performance, and operational results
Lead meetings and communicate across departments
Identify workflow problems and recommend improvements
Prepare reports and presentations for decision-makers
Coach employees and resolve workplace issues

education.graduate_school_note: A bachelor's degree is sufficient for many analyst, coordinator, operations, human resources, and project positions. An MBA or specialized master's degree may support consulting and senior leadership advancement, but work experience remains essential.
education.licensing_or_certification: No license is generally required. Project management, human resources, process improvement, and supply-chain certifications may become useful after students gain relevant experience.

salary.variability_note: Entry-level coordinators and associates may earn below this range. Experienced consultants, operations managers, human resources managers, and executives can earn substantially more.

advantages: Management skills apply across nearly every industry.
The field offers several entry routes through operations, projects, human resources, and consulting.
Strong performers can advance into positions with greater decision-making authority.
Professionals gain a broad understanding of how organizations function.
The experience can support entrepreneurship or nonprofit leadership.
tradeoffs: Graduates rarely enter true management positions immediately after college.
Managers are accountable for problems caused by their teams or systems.
Meetings, administrative work, and conflict resolution can consume significant time.
Project deadlines and client demands may require long hours or travel.
Leadership decisions sometimes involve incomplete information and competing priorities.
student_next_steps: Lead a defined project for a club, class, business, or community organization
Document the project's schedule, budget, problems, and final outcome
Practice running meetings and assigning clear responsibilities
Learn Excel and a basic project-management platform
Apply for operations, consulting, project, or management-development internships

tagline: Protect systems, information, and organizations from digital threats.
overview: Cybersecurity careers focus on preventing, detecting, investigating, and responding to attacks against computers, networks, applications, and data. Professionals monitor security alerts, test systems for weaknesses, investigate suspicious activity, manage access controls, and help organizations recover from incidents. The field includes technical roles such as penetration testing and digital forensics alongside risk, auditing, compliance, and security leadership positions.
career_themes: Preventing unauthorized access and data loss
typical_tasks: Monitor network, system, and application security alerts
Investigate suspicious logins, files, or network traffic
Test systems and applications for vulnerabilities
Configure access controls, firewalls, and security tools
Document incidents and recommend corrective actions
Explain security risks to technical and nontechnical teams

education.graduate_school_note: A bachelor's degree and practical experience are sufficient for many security analyst, audit, risk, and incident-response positions. Graduate education is more useful for advanced research, cryptography, architecture, and leadership roles.
education.licensing_or_certification: No universal license is required. Security, networking, cloud, and audit certifications may support employment. Government and defense positions may require a background investigation or security clearance.

salary.variability_note: Entry-level audit, support, and risk positions may fall below this range. Experienced security engineers, penetration testers, architects, and security leaders may earn substantially more.

advantages: Cybersecurity skills are needed across government, finance, healthcare, technology, and consulting.
The work protects real systems, information, and people from measurable risks.
Students can build practical experience through labs, competitions, and security projects.
The field offers technical, investigative, policy, audit, and leadership paths.
Many responsibilities can be performed remotely.
tradeoffs: Security incidents may require emergency or after-hours work.
Small mistakes can expose sensitive information or disrupt an organization.
Threats and security tools change constantly.
Many jobs advertised as entry-level still expect prior IT or networking experience.
Government and defense positions may involve background checks and workplace restrictions.
student_next_steps: Build a legal home lab using virtual machines and isolated networks
Learn Linux, networking fundamentals, and basic scripting
Complete beginner capture-the-flag security challenges
Document a vulnerability assessment or incident investigation
Apply for security, IT audit, risk, or network-support internships

tagline: Keep the technology people and organizations depend on working.
overview: Information technology careers focus on installing, maintaining, connecting, and improving the systems an organization uses every day. Professionals configure computers and networks, manage accounts and cloud services, troubleshoot technical problems, protect backups, support users, and plan system upgrades. Unlike software development, IT work usually emphasizes operating and supporting existing technology rather than building an application from the ground up.
career_themes: Managing accounts, devices, and cloud services
typical_tasks: Install and configure computers, software, and network equipment
Create user accounts and manage access permissions
Troubleshoot device, application, and connectivity problems
Monitor system performance, backups, and availability
Document technical issues and their solutions
Plan upgrades and coordinate changes with users or vendors

education.graduate_school_note: Graduate school is not generally needed for support, systems, networking, infrastructure, or operations roles. Practical experience and certifications are usually more valuable until a professional pursues architecture or senior leadership.
education.licensing_or_certification: No license is generally required. Certifications in networking, cloud platforms, operating systems, and technical support can strengthen entry-level applications.

salary.variability_note: Help-desk and user-support positions may begin near or below the minimum. Experienced systems engineers, network architects, cloud specialists, and IT leaders can earn substantially more.

advantages: Nearly every industry depends on IT systems and support.
Students can enter through support, networking, cloud, database, or systems roles.
Home labs and certifications provide practical experience outside an internship.
Technical problems often have concrete and visible solutions.
Experience can lead into cybersecurity, cloud architecture, systems engineering, or IT leadership.
tradeoffs: System failures may require evening, weekend, or on-call work.
User-support responsibilities can involve frustrated or impatient people.
Some work must be completed on-site around physical equipment.
Routine maintenance, account management, and documentation can become repetitive.
Professionals must continually learn new platforms and replace outdated certifications.
student_next_steps: Build a home lab with Windows, Linux, users, and shared resources
Learn basic networking, command-line, and troubleshooting skills
Document several technical problems and how they were resolved
Practice supporting real users through campus or volunteer work
Apply for help-desk, infrastructure, network, or systems internships

tagline: Evaluate money, investments, and risk to guide financial decisions.
overview: Finance careers focus on how individuals and organizations raise, invest, protect, and allocate money. Professionals evaluate companies, build financial models, analyze investment opportunities, assess credit and risk, manage portfolios, and advise clients or executives. The work ranges from relationship-driven financial advising to technical forecasting and quantitative investment research.
typical_tasks: Review financial statements, market data, and economic conditions
Build forecasts, budgets, and valuation models
Assess credit, investment, or portfolio risk
Prepare reports and recommendations for clients or managers
Monitor investments and compare performance with benchmarks
Present financial findings and defend assumptions

education.graduate_school_note: A bachelor's degree is sufficient for many analyst, credit, treasury, advising, and investment positions. Graduate education is more valuable for quantitative finance, advanced research, executive leadership, and some investment roles.
education.licensing_or_certification: There is no universal finance license. Securities, brokerage, and advisory positions may require employer-sponsored FINRA registration. Credentials such as CFA, CFP, and FRM are role-specific and usually pursued after entering the field.

salary.variability_note: Compensation varies sharply by role, location, employer, bonuses, and performance. Entry-level positions may fall below this range, while investment banking, quantitative finance, portfolio management, and senior leadership can exceed it substantially.

advantages: Finance skills apply across banking, investing, insurance, real estate, government, and corporate planning.
The field offers both quantitative and client-facing career paths.
Financial models and investment reports create concrete portfolio evidence.
Strong performance can lead to substantial compensation and responsibility.
Professionals develop an applied understanding of companies, markets, and economic decisions.
tradeoffs: Some roles require long hours, strict deadlines, and constant performance pressure.
Bonuses and job stability may depend on markets or company results.
Competitive positions often require internships and strong technical preparation.
Licensing or professional examinations may be required for certain paths.
Poor analysis or unethical recommendations can create major financial consequences.
student_next_steps: Build a financial model for a publicly traded company
Write a short investment or credit recommendation
Practice Excel, financial statements, and valuation methods
Join a student investment fund or finance organization
Apply for banking, corporate finance, investment, or risk internships

tagline: Test questions with evidence and turn observations into reliable knowledge.
overview: Science and research careers investigate how natural, medical, environmental, and physical systems work. Professionals design studies, collect samples, operate laboratory or field equipment, analyze results, and communicate what the evidence supports. Bachelor's-level graduates often begin as technicians, coordinators, or research assistants, while independent research and laboratory leadership commonly require graduate education.
typical_tasks: Review previous research and define a testable question
Prepare samples, materials, instruments, or study participants
Follow experimental procedures and safety requirements
Record observations and maintain detailed research notes
Analyze results and check them for errors or bias
Write reports, posters, papers, or research presentations

education.graduate_school_note: A bachelor's degree can lead to technician, laboratory, research-assistant, and project-coordination positions. Independent research, advanced specialization, university teaching, and laboratory leadership frequently require a master's degree or Ph.D.
education.licensing_or_certification: No universal research license is required. Clinical laboratories, regulated testing environments, animal research, and specialized equipment may require occupation-specific training or certification.

salary.variability_note: Technicians and academic research assistants may earn near or below the minimum. Experienced scientists in biotechnology, pharmaceuticals, government, computing, and research management may earn substantially more.

advantages: The work contributes to practical knowledge in health, technology, environment, and industry.
Students can explore several specialties before committing to graduate school.
Research experience strengthens applications for technical employment and advanced study.
Projects develop transferable skills in data, writing, experimentation, and problem solving.
The field rewards curiosity and sustained investigation.
tradeoffs: Many independent scientist positions require graduate education.
Experiments may fail or produce unclear results after significant preparation.
Academic and nonprofit research can depend on temporary grants or contracts.
Laboratory procedures and documentation may become repetitive.
Some positions involve hazardous materials, biological samples, or difficult field conditions.
student_next_steps: Ask a Loyola professor about assisting with an active research project
Develop statistics, laboratory, and research-writing skills
Maintain a detailed lab notebook or research log
Present a project through a poster, report, or student conference
Apply for laboratory, field, clinical-research, or summer research positions

tagline: Design the circuits, signals, controls, and power systems behind modern technology.
overview: Electrical engineering fits students who enjoy using math and physics to understand how electronic and power systems work. Professionals in this field design circuits, control systems, communication equipment, sensors, power networks, and other electrical technologies. The work usually combines computer simulation with laboratory testing, technical documentation, and collaboration with manufacturing or engineering teams.
typical_tasks: Create circuit diagrams and technical specifications
Simulate circuits before building hardware
Test prototypes with oscilloscopes and meters
Analyze signal, voltage, and power data
Troubleshoot electrical system failures
Document test results and design changes

education.graduate_school_note: A graduate degree can help with advanced work in signal processing, semiconductor design, communications, controls, power systems, and research. Most entry-level engineering positions begin with a bachelor's degree.
education.licensing_or_certification: No universal license is required. A Professional Engineer license may be required when independently offering engineering services to the public. The usual licensing path begins with the FE exam and EIT status.

salary.variability_note: The BLS reported a May 2024 median of $111,910 for electrical engineers and $127,590 for electronics engineers except computer. Semiconductor, aerospace, research, and senior power roles can pay more.

advantages: Electrical systems are used in energy, electronics, aerospace, communications, robotics, transportation, and medical technology.
Projects produce tangible circuits, devices, and systems that students can demonstrate in a portfolio.
The field offers strong compensation and several technical specialization paths.
Electrical knowledge transfers well into computer engineering, automation, and embedded systems.
Internships and laboratory projects provide direct opportunities to test career fit.
tradeoffs: The coursework requires sustained work in calculus, physics, circuits, and differential equations.
Hardware failures can be expensive or dangerous, making accuracy and safety procedures important.
Some positions require laboratory, manufacturing, utility, or customer-site work.
Testing and troubleshooting may take longer than the original design.
Engineers must keep up with changing hardware, software, and industry standards.
student_next_steps: Build and test a small circuit on a breadboard
Practice using a multimeter and oscilloscope
Simulate a circuit in LTspice or MATLAB
Join an engineering design or robotics team
Apply for an electronics, power, or controls internship

tagline: Design physical systems and improve how products and services are produced.
overview: This category combines two related but distinct paths. Mechanical engineers design and test machines, products, thermal systems, and mechanical components. Industrial engineers improve production, quality, workflow, logistics, and the use of people and equipment. It fits students who enjoy solving practical problems and want to make a product or process safer, faster, more reliable, or less expensive.
career_themes: Working with thermal and fluid systems
typical_tasks: Create CAD models and engineering drawings
Calculate forces, temperatures, and material behavior
Build and test mechanical prototypes
Analyze production time, cost, and quality data
Plan equipment layouts and workflows
Recommend design or process improvements

education.graduate_school_note: A bachelor's degree supports most entry-level engineering positions. Graduate study is more valuable for advanced simulation, robotics, aerospace, thermal systems, human factors, optimization, or research-heavy roles.
education.licensing_or_certification: Licensing depends on the position. A Professional Engineer license is important when providing engineering services directly to the public. Lean Six Sigma and quality certifications can be useful in industrial and manufacturing roles.

salary.variability_note: The BLS reported May 2024 median wages of $102,320 for mechanical engineers and $101,140 for industrial engineers. Aerospace, research, management, and specialized manufacturing positions can exceed this range.

advantages: Students can work on physical products, machines, production systems, or organization-wide processes.
Mechanical and industrial skills apply across manufacturing, aerospace, transportation, energy, healthcare, and logistics.
CAD models, prototypes, simulations, and process studies can become strong portfolio projects.
The category supports both technical design and operations leadership paths.
Students can specialize without abandoning the broader engineering foundation.
tradeoffs: The curriculum requires substantial calculus, physics, mechanics, and technical problem-solving.
Manufacturing positions may require regular time on production floors or at facilities.
Production failures and deadlines can create pressure to solve problems quickly.
Physical prototypes require more time and money to revise than many digital projects.
Some employers expect experience with industry-specific software, equipment, or quality standards.
student_next_steps: Create a working CAD assembly in SolidWorks
Analyze a mechanical system with MATLAB or ANSYS
Build and test a physical prototype
Complete a process-improvement or quality project
Apply for a manufacturing, design, or operations internship

tagline: Plan and improve the structures and infrastructure communities rely on.
overview: Civil engineering fits students who want to work on buildings, roads, bridges, transportation networks, construction sites, water systems, and community infrastructure. Civil engineers use structural calculations, drawings, maps, site information, budgets, and regulations to turn plans into safe projects. The work commonly moves between an office and active project sites.
typical_tasks: Prepare site plans and engineering drawings
Calculate structural loads and material requirements
Review survey, soil, traffic, or water data
Check designs against codes and permit requirements
Estimate project costs and construction schedules
Inspect construction progress at project sites

education.graduate_school_note: A bachelor's degree is the standard entry point. Graduate education becomes more valuable in structural, geotechnical, transportation, water-resource, and research-focused specializations.
education.licensing_or_certification: Professional Engineer licensing is important in civil engineering and is commonly required to approve plans or provide services directly to the public. The usual path includes an accredited degree, the FE exam, EIT status, qualifying experience, and the PE exam.

salary.variability_note: The BLS reported a May 2024 median wage of $99,590 for civil engineers. Government, consulting, specialized design, project leadership, and licensed positions can produce different compensation.

advantages: Projects create visible results such as roads, buildings, water systems, and public spaces.
Civil engineers can work for consulting firms, construction companies, developers, utilities, or government agencies.
Infrastructure needs create work across cities, suburbs, and rural communities.
The field offers clear specialization and professional licensing paths.
The work connects engineering decisions to public safety and community development.
tradeoffs: Site visits may involve weather, travel, noise, or active construction conditions.
Design decisions carry public-safety, legal, and financial responsibility.
Codes, permits, contracts, and government procedures can slow projects.
Large infrastructure projects may take years to complete.
Professional advancement may require licensing exams and documented experience.
student_next_steps: Create a basic site plan in CAD or GIS
Study a local transportation or infrastructure problem
Visit a construction or public-works project
Learn how the FE and PE licensing process works
Apply for an engineering, construction, planning, or government internship

tagline: Use engineering to understand human movement and design safer medical technology.
overview: Biomechanical engineering focuses on forces, motion, materials, and mechanical devices that interact with the human body. Students may study how joints move, how injuries occur, or how prosthetics, implants, rehabilitation equipment, surgical tools, and exoskeletons should perform. The field combines mechanical design, biology, data collection, laboratory testing, and medical-device safety.
typical_tasks: Collect motion, force, or pressure data
Design medical components in CAD
Simulate forces on implants or body structures
Build and test assistive-device prototypes
Evaluate device safety and performance
Document results for engineering or regulatory teams

education.graduate_school_note: A bachelor's degree can support entry-level medical-device, testing, manufacturing, and quality roles. A master's degree or doctorate is often valuable for specialized biomechanics research, advanced implant design, rehabilitation engineering, and university research.
education.licensing_or_certification: There is no universal biomechanical engineering license. A PE license applies to some engineering positions, while medical-device employers may value experience with FDA requirements, design controls, quality systems, and human-subject research procedures.

salary.variability_note: The BLS reported a May 2024 median wage of $106,950 for bioengineers and biomedical engineers. Pay varies across medical-device manufacturing, engineering services, healthcare support, research, and advanced product leadership.

advantages: The work connects engineering directly to mobility, rehabilitation, injury prevention, and patient care.
Students can create tangible projects involving prosthetics, wearable sensors, sports equipment, or assistive devices.
The field combines mechanics, biology, materials, software, and product design.
Career options exist in medical devices, sports technology, rehabilitation, research, and advanced manufacturing.
Biomechanics projects can provide strong preparation for graduate research.
tradeoffs: The job market is narrower than general mechanical engineering or software development.
Specialized research and development positions may require graduate education.
Medical-device testing and regulatory approval can make development slower.
Design errors can affect patient safety, increasing the need for careful validation.
Many projects require access to laboratories, testing equipment, or clinical partners.
recommended_course_ids: Physics of Medicine and the Human Body
Waves and the Physics of Medicine
student_next_steps: Complete a motion or force analysis project
Design a simple assistive device in CAD
Learn MATLAB or Python for biomechanical data
Ask a professor about biomechanics research
Apply for a medical-device, rehabilitation, or sports-technology internship

tagline: Build the software systems people and organizations use.
overview: Computer science and software development fit students who enjoy turning problems into working programs. Developers build websites, mobile applications, backend services, automation tools, databases, and large software systems. The work includes understanding user needs, designing a solution, writing code, testing it, fixing problems, deploying updates, and maintaining the product after release.
typical_tasks: Turn product requirements into technical plans
Write and review program code
Create automated tests and fix defects
Connect applications to databases and APIs
Deploy software and monitor performance
Document systems for users and developers

education.graduate_school_note: A bachelor's degree is common, but a strong portfolio and relevant experience can also influence hiring. Graduate study is more valuable for research, advanced machine learning, computer science theory, and certain specialized systems roles.
education.licensing_or_certification: No professional license is generally required. Cloud, security, or platform certifications can support specific positions, but working projects and technical experience usually matter more for software-development hiring.

salary.variability_note: The BLS reported May 2024 medians of $133,080 for software developers and $90,930 for web developers. Compensation varies substantially by specialization, experience, employer, location, and equity-based pay.

advantages: Students can build portfolio projects with a computer and low-cost development tools.
Software skills apply across finance, healthcare, government, entertainment, education, and engineering.
Many positions support remote or hybrid work.
The field offers strong compensation and several technical career paths.
Students can test their interest early by building and releasing a small application.
tradeoffs: Developers must continually learn new tools, platforms, and programming practices.
Debugging can require long periods of focused and repetitive work.
Technical interviews may require separate preparation in algorithms and system design.
Deadlines, outages, or on-call schedules can create periods of high pressure.
Hiring and compensation can change quickly across technology sectors.
student_next_steps: Build and deploy a small web or mobile application
Publish code with documentation and tests on GitHub
Practice data structures and debugging
Learn how to connect an application to a database and API
Apply for a software internship or contribute to an open-source project

tagline: Build the hardware and low-level software inside computing devices.
overview: Computer engineering combines electrical engineering and computer science. Computer engineers work with processors, digital circuits, embedded systems, firmware, sensors, FPGA designs, and the interfaces connecting hardware to software. It fits students who want to understand what happens below an application and enjoy testing physical devices as well as writing code.
typical_tasks: Design digital circuits or processor components
Write firmware and hardware-description code
Simulate logic before building hardware
Test boards, processors, and device interfaces
Debug timing, memory, and communication problems
Document hardware and verification results

education.graduate_school_note: A bachelor's degree is the standard entry point. Graduate study becomes more useful for advanced processor architecture, semiconductor design, integrated circuits, hardware acceleration, and research positions.
education.licensing_or_certification: No general professional license is required for most computer-engineering positions. A PE license applies only to certain public-facing engineering roles. Vendor certifications may help in specialized embedded or hardware platforms but are not universal.

salary.variability_note: The BLS reported a May 2024 median wage of $155,020 for computer hardware engineers. Semiconductor, processor, research, and senior architecture positions can exceed the listed range.

advantages: The field provides experience with both physical hardware and software.
Computer engineers can work in semiconductors, robotics, vehicles, aerospace, medical devices, communications, and consumer electronics.
Microcontroller and FPGA projects produce concrete portfolio evidence.
Hardware expertise can lead to specialized and well-paid engineering positions.
The degree can support movement into electrical engineering, embedded software, or systems engineering.
tradeoffs: The curriculum combines demanding topics from programming, circuits, digital logic, and mathematics.
Hardware changes are slower and more expensive than editing software.
Many positions require access to laboratories, development boards, or manufacturing equipment.
Semiconductor and advanced hardware jobs may be concentrated in particular regions.
Small timing, power, or component errors can prevent an entire system from working.
student_next_steps: Build a microcontroller or FPGA project
Practice C, C++, Verilog, or VHDL
Use an oscilloscope or logic analyzer to debug a circuit
Document code, schematics, and test results in one portfolio project
Apply for an embedded systems, hardware, firmware, or semiconductor internship

tagline: Use data and economic reasoning to understand markets, policy, and human decisions.
overview: Economics fits students who want to understand why prices change, how businesses respond to incentives, what drives employment and inflation, and how government decisions affect people. The work often involves collecting data, testing explanations, forecasting future conditions, and turning the results into recommendations for businesses, investors, nonprofits, or public agencies.
typical_tasks: Collect employment, price, market, or consumer data
Build regression and forecasting models
Estimate how a policy could affect different groups
Compare the costs and benefits of possible decisions
Create charts and reports for decision-makers
Explain model results without relying on technical language

education.graduate_school_note: A bachelor's degree can lead to analyst, consulting, finance, market research, and policy-support positions. Jobs carrying the formal title of economist often require a master's degree, while university research generally requires a doctorate.
education.licensing_or_certification: No professional license is generally required. Strong econometrics, programming, research, and writing experience usually matters more than certification.

salary.variability_note: The BLS reported a May 2024 median of $115,440 for economists. Entry-level analyst roles may pay less, while experienced economists in finance, consulting, technology, and government can earn more.

advantages: Economic reasoning applies to business, finance, government, healthcare, technology, and environmental policy.
Students learn to connect data with real decisions instead of only reporting numbers.
Economics combines well with statistics, data science, finance, political science, and business.
Research papers and forecasting projects can become useful portfolio samples.
The field supports both quantitative and policy-focused career paths.
tradeoffs: The formal economist job market is much smaller than the broader market for business and data analysts.
Many research-heavy positions require graduate education.
Economic models simplify reality and can produce weak conclusions when assumptions are unrealistic.
Forecasts are uncertain and must be updated when conditions change.
Students who avoid statistics and programming may have fewer career options.
student_next_steps: Use FRED or BLS data to answer one economic question
Build a regression or forecasting project in Stata, R, or Python
Write a one-page policy or market recommendation
Join a research, consulting, finance, or data project
Apply for an analyst internship before targeting economist positions

tagline: Measure environmental problems and help organizations reduce their impact.
overview: Environmental work fits students who want to address pollution, climate risk, conservation, land use, sustainable business, or environmental policy. Depending on the role, professionals may collect soil and water samples, map environmental conditions, review permits, calculate emissions, inspect facilities, or help an organization reduce waste and energy use. The category includes scientific, regulatory, business, and community-facing paths.
typical_tasks: Collect and analyze soil, water, air, or emissions data
Map environmental risks with GIS
Review permits and environmental regulations
Calculate an organization's emissions or resource use
Inspect facilities for environmental compliance
Recommend practical sustainability improvements

education.graduate_school_note: A bachelor's degree supports many environmental science, compliance, sustainability, GIS, and program roles. Graduate study becomes more valuable for advanced climate modeling, toxicology, research, environmental economics, and specialized policy work.
education.licensing_or_certification: No universal license applies across the category. Environmental engineers may pursue PE licensure. GIS, LEED, hazardous-material, auditing, and sustainability credentials can support specific positions.

salary.variability_note: The BLS reported a May 2024 median of $80,060 for environmental scientists and specialists. Environmental engineering, consulting, corporate sustainability, and management roles may pay more than field technician or nonprofit positions.

advantages: The work can produce measurable improvements in pollution, energy use, conservation, and public health.
Career options exist in government, consulting, engineering, nonprofits, research, and private companies.
Students can combine environmental interests with data, policy, business, law, or communication.
Fieldwork and campus sustainability projects provide accessible ways to test career fit.
GIS maps, environmental assessments, and emissions reports can become portfolio projects.
tradeoffs: Some positions involve outdoor work, travel, hazardous sites, or uncomfortable weather.
Environmental progress may be limited by budgets, politics, and regulatory delays.
Entry-level nonprofit and field positions may pay less than corporate or engineering roles.
Sustainability titles are inconsistent, so similar jobs may require very different skills.
Advanced climate and scientific research usually requires graduate education.
student_next_steps: Map a local environmental problem using GIS
Measure waste, energy, or water use for a campus organization
Practice collecting and documenting environmental samples
Volunteer with a conservation or environmental justice project
Apply for a government, consulting, nonprofit, or sustainability internship

tagline: Track financial activity and verify that organizations report it accurately.
overview: Accounting fits students who are comfortable working with financial records, detailed rules, and deadlines. Accountants record transactions, prepare financial statements, calculate taxes, test internal controls, and investigate whether records are accurate. Their work helps managers, investors, regulators, and clients understand where money came from, where it went, and whether the organization followed required standards.
typical_tasks: Record and classify business transactions
Reconcile bank and ledger balances
Prepare financial statements and supporting schedules
Test transactions during an audit
Calculate tax obligations and filing adjustments
Explain financial issues to managers or clients

education.graduate_school_note: A bachelor's degree supports staff accounting, audit, tax, and corporate accounting roles. Additional graduate coursework can help students meet CPA education requirements or move into specialized taxation, forensic accounting, and information-systems work.
education.licensing_or_certification: A CPA license is not required for every accounting job, but it is important for public accounting and certain advancement paths. CPA education and experience requirements vary by state. CMA, CIA, and CISA credentials support management accounting, internal audit, and technology-audit roles.

salary.variability_note: The BLS reported a May 2024 median of $81,680 for accountants and auditors. CPA status, industry specialization, management responsibility, and public-accounting experience can raise compensation.

advantages: Nearly every organization needs accounting, reporting, tax, or audit support.
The field offers clear entry-level positions and structured advancement paths.
Accounting knowledge transfers into finance, consulting, compliance, analytics, and management.
Students can demonstrate their skills through reconciliations, financial statements, and audit projects.
Professional credentials can provide a visible career advantage.
tradeoffs: Tax season, audits, quarter-end, and year-end reporting can require long hours.
Small errors can affect financial statements, taxes, or regulatory filings.
Some tasks are repetitive and governed by detailed procedures.
CPA eligibility and testing require substantial additional work.
Accounting standards, tax rules, and reporting technology change regularly.
student_next_steps: Build financial statements from a sample transaction file
Practice reconciliations and lookup formulas in Excel
Volunteer with a supervised tax-preparation program
Check Maryland CPA education requirements before senior year
Apply for audit, tax, corporate accounting, or internal-control internships

tagline: Use mathematical models and data to solve problems that cannot be answered by intuition alone.
overview: Mathematics and statistics fit students who enjoy working carefully through difficult problems and explaining why an answer is valid. Applied work may involve designing experiments, estimating risk, testing medical treatments, forecasting demand, or optimizing a system. Pure mathematics focuses more heavily on proofs, structures, and the logical foundations later used in computing, economics, physics, and cryptography.
typical_tasks: Choose an appropriate model for a research question
Clean and validate data before analysis
Calculate estimates and uncertainty intervals
Design experiments or sampling plans
Write code to run simulations and models
Present results through tables, graphs, and explanations

education.graduate_school_note: A bachelor's degree can lead to actuarial, analytics, operations research, programming, and junior statistical roles. Formal mathematician and statistician positions frequently require a master's degree, while university research generally requires a doctorate.
education.licensing_or_certification: No general professional license is required. Actuarial careers require a sequence of professional examinations. Certifications in statistical software are optional and usually less important than applied project experience.

salary.variability_note: The BLS reported May 2024 medians of $121,680 for mathematicians and $103,300 for statisticians. Compensation varies across government, insurance, healthcare, technology, finance, and academic research.

advantages: Mathematical and statistical skills transfer across science, finance, healthcare, government, engineering, and technology.
Students learn methods for handling uncertainty instead of relying on guesses.
Programming and domain knowledge can turn the degree into several applied career paths.
Research and modeling projects provide measurable portfolio evidence.
The field provides strong preparation for quantitative graduate programs.
tradeoffs: A degree built around theory alone may not communicate job readiness to employers.
Formal mathematician and statistician roles often require graduate education.
Proof-based courses demand a different style of thinking from routine calculation.
Incorrect assumptions or poor data can invalidate an otherwise correct model.
Students need programming and communication skills to access the widest range of jobs.
student_next_steps: Complete one statistical analysis using a public dataset
Learn R or Python well enough to reproduce the analysis
Write a short explanation of the assumptions and limitations
Enter a modeling, analytics, or actuarial competition
Apply for research, actuarial, operations, or analytics internships

tagline: Develop and test the metals, polymers, ceramics, and composites used in real products.
overview: Materials engineering fits students who want to understand why physical materials bend, crack, corrode, conduct heat, or survive demanding conditions. Materials engineers select and modify metals, polymers, ceramics, composites, and electronic materials for products such as aircraft, batteries, medical implants, buildings, and computer chips. The work combines laboratory testing, chemistry, physics, manufacturing, and failure analysis.
typical_tasks: Test material strength, hardness, corrosion, or heat resistance
Examine samples with microscopes and laboratory instruments
Compare materials against product requirements
Investigate why a component cracked or failed
Adjust manufacturing or heat-treatment procedures
Document test methods and recommend material changes

education.graduate_school_note: A bachelor's degree supports entry-level testing, manufacturing, quality, and materials engineering positions. Graduate study is more valuable for nanotechnology, semiconductor materials, battery research, biomaterials, and advanced materials development.
education.licensing_or_certification: No universal materials-engineering license is required. A PE license applies to some public-facing engineering work. Specialized testing, welding, quality, and nondestructive-evaluation credentials may help in particular industries.

salary.variability_note: The BLS reported a May 2024 median of $108,310 for materials engineers. Semiconductor, aerospace, research, and senior product-development roles can pay more.

advantages: Materials decisions affect products in aerospace, energy, medicine, electronics, construction, and transportation.
Laboratory tests produce direct evidence students can include in technical portfolios.
The field connects chemistry and physics to real manufacturing problems.
Students can specialize in metals, polymers, ceramics, composites, biomaterials, or electronic materials.
Failure analysis gives the work a clear investigative component.
tradeoffs: Many positions require regular laboratory or manufacturing-site access.
Advanced research roles may require a master's degree or doctorate.
Testing can be repetitive because results must be verified under several conditions.
Material and manufacturing failures can create serious safety or financial consequences.
Specialized equipment may limit the projects students can complete independently.
student_next_steps: Compare two materials using a documented laboratory test
Write a failure-analysis report for a broken component
Learn microscopy, hardness testing, or tensile testing
Ask an engineering or physics professor about materials research
Apply for a manufacturing, quality, aerospace, or laboratory internship

tagline: Help people learn by designing instruction, guiding practice, and measuring progress.
overview: Education fits students who enjoy explaining ideas, supporting other people, and adjusting their approach when someone does not understand. Teachers and education professionals plan lessons, lead activities, assess learning, manage group behavior, and communicate with students, families, and colleagues. The category also includes academic advising, admissions, training, instructional design, and education policy.
typical_tasks: Set clear learning goals
Create lessons, activities, and practice materials
Explain the same idea in different ways
Assess student work and provide feedback
Maintain records and communicate progress
Adjust instruction for different learning needs

education.graduate_school_note: A bachelor's degree and state-approved preparation can lead to classroom teaching. Instructional coordination, school leadership, counseling, and university teaching usually require graduate education and prior professional experience.
education.licensing_or_certification: Public-school teachers generally need state licensure for their grade level or subject. Requirements vary by state. Private-school, corporate-training, tutoring, and some instructional-design roles may not require a teaching license.

salary.variability_note: The BLS reported May 2024 medians of $64,580 for high school teachers and $74,720 for instructional coordinators. Pay depends heavily on the role, school system, contract, location, education level, and experience.

advantages: Educators can see how their work affects student knowledge, confidence, and opportunities.
Teaching skills transfer into training, advising, instructional design, nonprofit work, and management.
Students can test their interest through tutoring or classroom observation before committing to licensure.
The field offers subject-specific, age-specific, administrative, and technology-focused paths.
Lesson plans and learning materials provide concrete portfolio evidence.
tradeoffs: Teaching requires substantial preparation, grading, documentation, and communication outside lesson time.
Classroom management can be emotionally demanding.
Public-school roles require state-specific licensing and background checks.
Compensation may not match the workload in some districts or nonprofit settings.
Advanced administration and curriculum roles usually require graduate study and prior experience.
student_next_steps: Tutor or mentor one student consistently
Create and teach a short lesson with a clear learning goal
Observe a classroom or educational program
Review Maryland licensing requirements for the subject and age group
Apply for a school, camp, tutoring, advising, or training position

tagline: Research, verify, and shape information into writing people can understand and use.
overview: Writing and journalism fit students who enjoy finding the right information and presenting it clearly for a specific audience. Journalists interview sources, verify claims, review public records, and report what happened. Writers and editors may create articles, reports, speeches, technical guides, marketing copy, books, or digital content. Across these roles, published work and proven reliability matter as much as the degree itself.
career_themes: Publishing across digital and print media
typical_tasks: Research a topic using documents and credible sources
Interview people who have direct knowledge
Write articles, reports, scripts, or guides
Check names, dates, quotations, and supporting evidence
Revise work to meet editorial requirements
Prepare content for web, print, audio, or video publication

education.graduate_school_note: A bachelor's degree is common, but employers usually place heavy weight on published clips, internships, subject knowledge, and editing ability. Graduate study is more useful for specialized reporting, advanced technical writing, academia, or a major career change.
education.licensing_or_certification: No professional license is generally required. A strong portfolio of published work is usually more valuable than a general writing certification.

salary.variability_note: The BLS reported May 2024 medians of $60,280 for journalists, $72,270 for writers and authors, and $75,260 for editors. Technical writing, management, freelancing, location, and subject specialization create substantial variation.

advantages: Writing skills transfer into journalism, publishing, business, science, government, marketing, and nonprofit work.
Students can begin building a portfolio through campus publications and independent reporting.
Subject expertise can create specialized paths in science, business, health, politics, or technology.
Many roles allow remote, freelance, or project-based work.
Published work gives employers direct evidence of research and communication ability.
tradeoffs: Entry-level journalism and publishing positions can be competitive and modestly paid.
Deadlines may require evening, weekend, or breaking-news work.
Freelance income can be inconsistent.
Writers must accept frequent editing, rejection, and revision.
Generative AI increases pressure on generic writing, making reporting, expertise, judgment, and original sourcing more important.
student_next_steps: Publish three polished clips in different formats
Report one original campus or Baltimore story
Practice interviewing and verifying information
Edit a draft using a professional style guide
Apply to a campus publication, newsroom, publisher, or communications internship

tagline: Turn public problems into research, policy proposals, campaigns, and government programs.
overview: Politics and public policy fit students who want to understand how governments make decisions and how those decisions affect communities. Professionals in this field research legislation, analyze budgets and public data, speak with community groups, prepare recommendations, and help elected officials, agencies, campaigns, or advocacy organizations act on an issue. The work is less about debating opinions and more about gathering evidence, understanding stakeholders, and working through real political and administrative limits.
typical_tasks: Research proposed laws and regulations
Write policy briefs and legislative summaries
Analyze demographic, budget, or polling data
Prepare officials for meetings and hearings
Coordinate campaign or advocacy events
Gather feedback from community stakeholders

education.graduate_school_note: A bachelor's degree can lead to campaign, legislative support, government affairs, nonprofit, and junior policy positions. Formal political scientist and advanced policy research roles often require a master's degree or doctorate.
education.licensing_or_certification: No general license is required. Planning roles may value AICP certification after qualifying education and experience. Data, GIS, budgeting, and program-evaluation skills are usually more useful than general political certifications.

salary.variability_note: The BLS reported May 2024 medians of $139,380 for political scientists and $83,720 for urban and regional planners. Campaign and entry-level nonprofit positions often pay less than research, consulting, management, and federal roles.

advantages: The work can influence legislation, government services, elections, and community investment.
Students can enter through campaigns, internships, advocacy organizations, or government offices.
Policy research combines writing, data, law, economics, and public communication.
Experience transfers between government, consulting, nonprofits, and corporate public affairs.
Policy briefs, polling analyses, and program evaluations can become portfolio evidence.
tradeoffs: Government and legislative changes can cancel or redirect projects.
Political progress is often slower than the underlying public problem.
Campaign work may require evenings, weekends, and unpredictable schedules.
Entry-level political and nonprofit positions may offer modest compensation.
Formal political science research positions are limited and often require graduate education.
recommended_course_ids: State and Local Politics and Policymaking
Constitutional Law: Federalism and Separation of Powers
student_next_steps: Write a one-page brief on a Maryland policy issue
Attend a city council, county, or legislative hearing
Volunteer for a campaign or advocacy organization
Analyze public budget, census, or polling data
Apply for a legislative, government, planning, or nonprofit internship

tagline: Research legal questions, organize evidence, and help people or organizations navigate the law.
overview: Legal services fit students who like reading closely, identifying what a rule actually says, and building an argument from evidence. Attorneys advise clients and represent them in negotiations or court. Paralegals, investigators, mediators, and program coordinators collect records, prepare documents, track deadlines, interview people, and support legal cases. Becoming an attorney requires law school and bar admission, but several legal-support careers do not.
typical_tasks: Research statutes, regulations, and court decisions
Summarize evidence and case history
Draft contracts, motions, or client correspondence
Track filing dates and legal deadlines
Interview clients, witnesses, or specialists
Prepare materials for negotiation, hearings, or trial

education.graduate_school_note: Paralegal, legal assistant, compliance, and program-support roles may begin with an associate or bachelor's degree. Practicing attorneys must earn a JD and satisfy state bar-admission requirements.
education.licensing_or_certification: Attorneys must be admitted to the bar in the jurisdiction where they practice. Paralegal certification is generally optional, although employers may prefer it. Mediation and court-interpreter requirements vary by state and court system.

salary.variability_note: The BLS reported May 2024 medians of $61,010 for paralegals and legal assistants and $151,160 for lawyers. Attorney compensation varies sharply by practice area, employer, location, and billable-hour expectations.

advantages: Legal work can directly protect rights, resolve disputes, and guide important decisions.
The field offers paths in government, corporations, courts, nonprofits, and private firms.
Legal research and writing transfer into compliance, policy, contracts, and consulting.
Students can test the field through legal aid, mock trial, internships, and court observation.
Attorneys can specialize in areas connected to technology, business, healthcare, media, or the environment.
tradeoffs: Becoming an attorney requires three additional years of school and potentially substantial debt.
Court filings and client matters involve strict deadlines and serious consequences.
Adversarial cases can be stressful and emotionally draining.
Large-firm attorney compensation often comes with long and unpredictable hours.
Legal work involves more reading, writing, and procedural detail than courtroom speaking.
recommended_course_ids: Constitutional Law: Federalism and Separation of Powers
Law, Lawyers, and Litigants in European History
student_next_steps: Brief a court case using facts, issue, rule, and holding
Observe a public court hearing
Volunteer with legal aid or a rights-focused nonprofit
Apply for a courthouse, law office, compliance, or paralegal internship
Compare JD cost and career outcomes before committing to law school

tagline: Use language and cultural knowledge to help people and organizations work across borders.
overview: Languages and international affairs fit students who want to communicate across cultures and understand how political, economic, and social conditions differ between countries. The work may involve translating documents, interpreting conversations, supporting diplomats, assisting international students or migrants, researching regional risks, or coordinating programs across several countries. Professional fluency requires sustained speaking, listening, reading, and writing practice beyond completing a few language courses.
career_themes: Researching global events and regional risks
typical_tasks: Translate documents while preserving their meaning
Interpret conversations in real time
Research political and cultural conditions in another country
Prepare international briefings and correspondence
Coordinate travel, visas, meetings, or overseas programs
Adapt communication for local cultural expectations

education.graduate_school_note: A bachelor's degree combined with strong language proficiency can support translation, international education, aid, localization, and program roles. Diplomacy, geopolitical research, and advanced international policy positions may prefer graduate education and relevant regional experience.
education.licensing_or_certification: No universal license is required. Court and medical interpreters may need jurisdiction-specific certification. Government and national-security positions may require citizenship, background investigations, or security clearances.

salary.variability_note: The BLS reported a May 2024 median of $59,440 for interpreters and translators. Government, localization, specialized legal or medical language work, and international management may pay more.

advantages: Language ability creates access to communities and information unavailable to monolingual workers.
International skills apply to diplomacy, business, education, migration, aid, media, and law.
Study abroad and community work provide direct ways to test the field.
Students can combine language proficiency with technical, business, legal, or healthcare knowledge.
Cross-cultural experience can support careers involving travel or international collaboration.
tradeoffs: Course completion alone rarely produces professional fluency.
Language ability without a second specialization may not create a clear career path.
Freelance translation and interpretation work can be inconsistent.
Interpretation requires fast, accurate decisions under pressure.
Government and overseas assignments may involve lengthy applications, relocation, or security requirements.
student_next_steps: Practice weekly conversation with fluent speakers
Measure proficiency using an ACTFL-aligned assessment
Create a reviewed translation or bilingual writing sample
Study abroad or volunteer with an immigrant-serving organization
Apply for an international education, aid, localization, or government internship

tagline: Research, preserve, and explain the records and objects that document the past.
overview: History and cultural heritage fit students who enjoy working with original evidence such as letters, photographs, government records, oral histories, buildings, artworks, and physical artifacts. Historians interpret what the evidence shows. Archivists organize and preserve records. Museum and preservation professionals care for objects, buildings, and collections while helping the public understand why they matter.
typical_tasks: Locate primary sources in archives and databases
Verify dates, names, ownership, and historical context
Describe records using searchable metadata
Handle and store historical materials safely
Interview people for oral-history projects
Create exhibits, tours, articles, or digital collections

education.graduate_school_note: A bachelor's degree can support museum assistant, records, research, and public-history positions. Professional historian, archivist, curator, and conservation roles commonly prefer or require a relevant master's degree.
education.licensing_or_certification: No general license is required. Archivists may pursue professional certification. Art conservation and advanced museum work frequently require specialized graduate education and supervised practical experience.

salary.variability_note: The BLS reported May 2024 medians of $74,050 for historians and $57,100 across archivists, curators, and museum workers. Senior management, consulting, and specialized preservation roles can pay more.

advantages: The work preserves records, objects, and stories that could otherwise be lost.
Students can build practical experience through archives, museums, oral histories, and digital exhibits.
Historical research supports careers in museums, law, government, education, media, and preservation.
Projects can create visible public resources rather than remaining classroom papers.
Students can specialize by region, time period, material, or type of institution.
tradeoffs: Museum, archive, and historian positions are competitive.
Many professional roles require graduate education despite modest salary levels.
Institutions may depend on grants, donations, or government funding.
Collections work can involve repetitive description and careful handling procedures.
Students need digital, project, or public-facing skills in addition to historical knowledge.
recommended_course_ids: Africa in the Age of Globalization
student_next_steps: Build a digital exhibit from primary sources
Record an oral history with consent and a transcript
Practice describing archival items with searchable metadata
Volunteer at a museum, archive, or historical society
Apply for public-history, preservation, records, or collections internships

tagline: Manage how an organization communicates with its audiences, employees, and the public.
overview: Media, communications, and public relations fit students who enjoy shaping messages and coordinating how information reaches different audiences. Professionals write press releases, pitch reporters, manage social channels, prepare executives for interviews, communicate with employees, and respond when an organization faces criticism or a crisis. Unlike journalism, the work represents an organization or client rather than independently reporting on it.
typical_tasks: Write press releases and executive talking points
Pitch stories to journalists and media outlets
Plan content across social and digital channels
Monitor coverage and audience response
Prepare communication during a crisis
Report campaign results to clients or leadership

education.graduate_school_note: A bachelor's degree and strong portfolio are sufficient for many entry-level communications and PR roles. Graduate education is generally more useful for career changes, specialized research, or senior strategic leadership.
education.licensing_or_certification: No professional license is required. Platform and analytics certifications may help with specific tools, but writing samples, campaign results, media experience, and professional judgment usually matter more.

salary.variability_note: The BLS reported May 2024 medians of $69,780 for public relations specialists and $138,520 for public relations managers. Industry, location, client responsibility, and management experience create substantial variation.

advantages: Communications work exists in corporations, government, healthcare, entertainment, education, and nonprofits.
Students can build experience through clubs, campus organizations, and local clients.
Campaigns produce measurable results and visible portfolio pieces.
The field combines writing, strategy, media, analytics, and relationship management.
Communication skills can support advancement into brand, public affairs, or executive leadership.
tradeoffs: Crises and negative coverage may require immediate responses outside normal hours.
Public mistakes can damage both the organization and the communicator's credibility.
Entry-level roles may involve heavy scheduling, monitoring, and administrative work.
Success is partly dependent on journalists, algorithms, and public reaction.
Professionals must separate personal opinions from the organization they represent.
recommended_course_ids: Fundamentals of Advertising and Public Relations
student_next_steps: Create a press release, media list, and social rollout for one event
Manage communication for a student organization and track results
Practice responding to a realistic crisis scenario
Pitch a genuine campus or community story to a publication
Apply for a PR, communications, public affairs, or social media internship

tagline: Turn visual, audio, performance, and design ideas into finished creative work.
overview: Arts and creative industries fit students who want to make work that people can see, hear, watch, use, or experience. Depending on the path, professionals may design graphics, record audio, film a documentary, build a theatrical set, illustrate medical information, create costumes, or shape a digital interface. Career progress depends heavily on the quality of the portfolio, the ability to complete projects on schedule, and reliable collaboration with clients and production teams.
typical_tasks: Develop sketches, scripts, storyboards, or mockups
Create work with design, editing, or production software
Present concepts and respond to feedback
Prepare files, equipment, sets, or assets for production
Coordinate with performers, clients, and technical teams
Revise and deliver finished creative work

education.graduate_school_note: A bachelor's degree can provide training and professional connections, but portfolio quality and production experience are central to hiring. Graduate education is more relevant for university teaching, art therapy, advanced research, and some specialized design fields.
education.licensing_or_certification: No general license is required. Art therapy and certain design professions may require graduate education or state-specific credentials. Software certificates rarely replace a strong portfolio.

salary.variability_note: The BLS reported a May 2024 median of $53,180 across arts and design occupations. Graphic designers had a $61,300 median, while experienced art directors had a $111,040 median. Freelance income can vary substantially.

advantages: Students can show employers completed work instead of relying only on grades.
Creative skills apply to entertainment, advertising, publishing, healthcare, education, and technology.
Freelance and independent work can provide additional ways to enter the field.
Projects combine personal expression with real production and client constraints.
Students can test several media before choosing a specialization.
tradeoffs: Creative job markets are competitive and often portfolio-driven.
Freelance and project-based income can be unstable.
Production schedules may require nights, weekends, travel, or long sessions.
Client feedback can override personal creative preferences.
Students must continually update both their portfolio and technical tools.
student_next_steps: Build a portfolio containing six to ten finished pieces
Complete one collaborative production with a real deadline
Learn one primary creative tool beyond basic tutorials
Submit work to an exhibition, festival, publication, or competition
Apply for production, design, gallery, studio, or creative-agency internships

tagline: Study how people think, behave, develop, and respond to groups, institutions, and environments.
overview: Social and behavioral sciences fit students who want to investigate human behavior using observation, interviews, surveys, experiments, and statistical analysis. Applied roles use this evidence to improve workplaces, products, health programs, public policy, or community services. Clinical psychologists diagnose and treat mental-health conditions, but that path requires doctoral education, supervised training, and state licensure.
typical_tasks: Design surveys, interviews, or behavioral studies
